title: MA8-10280
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The principal claimant, XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, his partner XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, their daughter XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, citizens of Colombia, and their sons XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX and XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, citizens of the United States of America, are claiming refugee protection in Canada under section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).

As per subsection 167(2) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) and Rule 15 of the Refugee Protection Division Rules, the principal claimant, XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, confirmed at the hearing that he accepted being the designed representative for his minor children.
Given the copies of the claimants' passports submitted on file,1 the panel is satisfied as to their identities.
The principal claimant alleged the following facts.
From XXXXX 1986 to XXXXX 1989, he worked as a XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX of XXXXX, Colombia.

He resigned from his position as a XXXXX XXXXX because of threats (telephone calls) received mostly at his mother's residence. According to the claimant, the authors of the threats were members of various popular militias (FARC, EPL and ELN). However, also according to the claimant, the authors of the threats never identified themselves.

The claimant stated that, after this resignation, he moved a number of times for his own safety and that during this time, he continued to receive telephone calls at his mother's home. However, the callers then tried to recruit the claimant for various popular militias instead of just uttering threats of reprisals because of his work as a XXXXX XXXXX.
From 1996 to 1997, he worked as a XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX of XXXXX, Columbia.

He resigned as a XXXXX XXXXX in 1997 because some members of various popular militias had found him. The claimant stated that he received a telephone threat at work during this time. The claimant stated that he resigned from that position for his own safety and that of his family.
From 1997 to 1999, he worked as a security XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, XXXXX Sector, XXXXX, Colombia.
He resigned as a XXXXX XXXXX in 1999 because of threats from different popular militias.

He did not file any complaint with the police or any other authorities in Colombia regarding these threats because the judicial institutions in Colombia have been infiltrated by the popular militias and filing a complaint would only have increased the dangers that he already faced.
He left Colombia for the United States of America in 2000 to join his wife XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX and his daughter XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX.
He returned to Colombia in XXXXX 2002 to see whether he could live there without being threatened and to obtain documents to facilitate a claim for asylum in the United States of America.

He returned to the United States of America in XXXXX 2003 in the hopes of filing a claim for asylum for himself and the members of his family. He then determined, after receiving advice from a number of lawyers, that his chances of success were better in Canada than in the United States of America.
He claimed refugee protection for himself and his family on XXXXX, 2008, at Lacolle, Quebec, Canada.

The claimants, XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX and XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, the minor sons of the claimants, are citizens of the United States of America. The claimants did not submit any evidence pertaining to their fear regarding the United States of America.

After examining all of the documentary and testimonial evidence, the panel determines that the claimants did not discharge their burden of demonstrating a "reasonable fear of persecution" should they return to Colombia. The panel also determines that the claimants have not demonstrated that, on a balance of probabilities, they would be "persons in need of protection".

The panel believes that an internal flight alternative is the determinative question in these claims for refugee protection. In reply to the question [translation] "What would you fear should you return to your country?" the principal claimant replied that he fears that the people who were trying to recruit him into the popular militias are still there and will try to recruit him again. The panel repeatedly asked whether specific and identifiable people might possibly present a danger to the claimants, but the claimants were not able to answer. According to the claimants, the threats were made anonymously over the telephone.

The documentary evidence2 on file demonstrates that in Colombia, recruitment by popular militias, more specifically the FARC, is conducted on a voluntary basis and that forced recruitment is prohibited. Candidates sought are usually illiterate and between the ages of 15 and 30. In this case, the claimant is almost 45 years old. Furthermore, nothing indicates that the claimant was forced to join one of these popular militias, at least not by any direct threat over the past 20 years. According to the claimant's testimony, the alleged authors of the telephone calls never stopped trying to recruit him, even though he left Colombia over 10 years ago. Also according to the claimant, his mother is still receiving telephone calls at her home inquiring as to the claimant's status and his interest in joining the popular militias. The panel is of the opinion that it is highly unlikely that the militias are still trying to recruit the claimant 10 years after his departure from Colombia. Furthermore, the claimant was not able to satisfy the panel that these attempts to recruit him could turn into reprisals if he did not acquiesce to this pressure to recruit him, since he was not subject to any direct threat and he did not submit any evidence to that effect. The panel concludes that the claimant's allegation that the alleged authors of the telephone calls continued to try to recruit him after he left Colombia and are still doing so today is implausible and therefore undermines the claimant's credibility.

Furthermore, at the hearing, the principal claimant was questioned about what he might fear should he return to live elsewhere in Columbia-in Bogota, for example. Although the panel ensured that the claimants were given the opportunity to present their evidence, they did not provide any reason as to why it would be unreasonable, as outlined by the jurisprudence,3 to return to their country to find refuge. Nor did they submit any real and concrete evidence establishing that current conditions are such that they would face persecution under one of the Convention grounds or a risk to their life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment.

The panel is of the opinion that the claimants could move to another city in Colombia. At his hearing, the principal claimant stated that he had not actually been threatened, but had been solicited by members of the popular militias after he resigned from the police force.

The panel is of the opinion that the claimants were not able to establish, on a balance of probabilities, that relocating within Colombia, more specifically to Bogota, would cause them to fear for their lives. The claimants' main argument is that the alleged authors of the telephone calls could find them anywhere in Colombia. The panel is of the opinion that it is highly unlikely that the popular militias would feel the need to find and pursue the principal claimant elsewhere in Colombia.

Consequently, the panel concludes that it is not objectively unreasonable to believe, or too harsh to expect, that the claimants could move to Bogota before claiming refugee protection abroad. The claimants were not able to prove that the alleged authors of the telephone calls would have any interest in pursuing or trying to find them. To the contrary, according to the principal claimant, the authors of the calls were attempting to recruit him to their organization. It is highly unlikely that the principal claimant could be of such interest to the alleged authors of the telephone calls that they would try to find him in Colombia, more specifically Bogota.

As mentioned by Justice Lagacé in Ramirez: "...the burden of proof regarding an internal flight alternative rests on the claimant...Thus, the applicant had to establish either that it would be unreasonable for her to seek refuge in another part of the country or that there were, in fact, conditions preventing her from relocating elsewhere..."4 In Palacios, Justice Shore reiterates that which has been repeatedly upheld by jurisprudence: "It is settled law that in matters concerning internal flight alternatives the burden of proof is on the applicant... Therefore, the refugee claimant must demonstrate that it would be unreasonable for him or her to seek refuge in a different part of the country."5 In Thirunavukkarasu,6 the Court of Appeal established that the onus is on the claimant to demonstrate why, on a balance of probabilities, they face a serious risk of persecution in a part of the country that could provide an internal flight alternative.

In this case, the panel is of the opinion that the claimants did not discharge their burden of proof as established by the jurisprudence7 and concludes that they have an internal flight alternative in Bogota, Colombia. As noted by Justice Shore in Palacios,8 this finding by the panel is sufficient in itself to dispose of the claim for refugee protection, regardless of whether the claim refers to section 96 or subsection 97(1) of the IRPA.

Consequently, the panel determines that the principal claimant and the members of his family are not "Convention refugees" or "persons in need of protection" under section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the IRPA.

For these reasons, their claims for refugee protection are rejected.
